name: Fruit & Vegetable Production

objectives.text: Sort fruits and vegetables by the plant part we eat, such as root, stem, leaf, flower, fruit, or seed
Identify fruits and vegetables grown in the local area and the season when each is harvested
Describe the life cycle of a vegetable plant from seed to harvest
Describe what a plant needs to produce a healthy fruit or vegetable crop, including sunlight, water, soil nutrients, and space
Distinguish cool-season from warm-season vegetables and explain when each is planted
Distinguish annual vegetable crops from perennial fruit and vegetable crops such as tree fruits, small fruits, and asparagus
Design a small vegetable garden plan showing crop placement, plant spacing, and planting dates
Explain how a fruit develops from the parts of a flower
Explain the role of pollination in fruit set and yield
Explain how frost dates, hardiness zones, and growing degree days guide crop and cultivar selection
Demonstrate direct seeding and field transplanting of vegetables using correct depth, spacing, and hardening off
Compare production practices for a fruit crop and a vegetable crop, including spacing, pruning, and harvest timing
Explain how training systems such as trellising, staking, and pruning affect yield and fruit quality
Describe the steps of growing a vegetable crop from crop and cultivar selection through land preparation, sowing, irrigation, fertilizing, and harvest
Plant and maintain a fruit or vegetable crop in a school plot or SAE using the appropriate production steps
Identify the components and functions of seeds and fruits and classify horticultural fruits as berries, drupes, pomes, aggregates, or multiples
Summarize sustainable soil management methods for vegetable production, including rotation by plant family, cover crops, companion planting, and mulching
Evaluate how seed and fruit structures influence the culture, harvest, and use of fruit and vegetable crops
Develop a nutrient management plan for a fruit or vegetable crop based on soil test results and crop nutrient needs
Compare drip, overhead, and furrow irrigation and fertigation for fruit and vegetable crops in terms of water use, disease risk, and cost
Assess maturity indices such as color, firmness, size, and soluble solids to determine when a fruit or vegetable crop is ready for harvest and market
Harvest and grade fruits and vegetables according to USDA grade standards and industry practices
Analyze ripening physiology, including climacteric and nonclimacteric fruit and the role of ethylene, to explain changes in produce quality
Evaluate the impact of respiration rate on postharvest handling decisions such as precooling, storage temperature, and shelf life
Explain how Good Agricultural Practices reduce microbial contamination of fresh produce during growing, harvest, and packing
Compare hand and mechanical harvesting of fruit and vegetable crops and demonstrate a mechanical harvesting practice
Explain how site selection, rootstock choice, and pollinizer cultivars are used to establish an orchard or small fruit planting
Evaluate the impact of genetically modified fruit and vegetable cultivars on other production practices
Analyze yield and loss records from a fruit or vegetable SAE or production trial
Recommend strategies to reduce field and postharvest losses based on fruit or vegetable yield and loss data
Evaluate a fruit or vegetable production system for profitability, quality control, and market readiness
Create a production and marketing plan for a fruit or vegetable SAE enterprise, including crop schedule, enterprise budget, and market channels

changes: Kept all six original objectives as real competencies, rewording the grade 2 sort to classify by plant part eaten and splitting the grade 10 quality objective into separate ripening physiology and respiration-based postharvest objectives. Added competencies the old template missed: local seasonality, plant life cycle, cool and warm season crops, annual and perennial crops, garden design, flower-to-fruit development, frost dates and hardiness zones, seeding and transplanting, training systems, fruit classification, nutrient management, irrigation, maturity indices, grading, GAP food safety, mechanical harvest, orchard establishment, GMO cultivars, yield and loss analysis, and SAE enterprise planning. Greenhouse transplant production, field crops, and pest management were left to the sibling sub-topics. Standards were assigned only to grade 9 to 12 objectives that directly teach them.
